EASTERN AFFAIRS AND THE GOVERNMENT. Tram has dared everything, and defied everybody, and the Conference, whose pro- gress, or want of progress, has for so many weeks riveted the attention of the whole of the civilised world is, at last, the property of history. The barbarian may be said to be muter of the situation, Turkey has at length essentially changed her position in relation to the rest of the world. It is now unique. Byrom said that "France got drunk with blood to vomit crime." Turkey in the drunken delirium, engendered by the innocent blood of Bulgaria, etrikes friend and foe indiscriminately, and is left alone in %wild isolation to recover her rea- son. andto find that she is a State in Europe, but not of it. Already there are eigne that the Rolittoal fever which has raged amongst Official Turkey is subsiding. A correspon- dent at Conatantinople, who speaks with authority, reports that —" Savfet Puha called on General Ignatieff on Tuesday, and told him that the Porte now proposes to carry out of its own accord all the reforms now demanded by the Conference. It has sent to Psris for sin gendarmes in order to eatabliah a sufficient gendarmerie, and to England for three or four official. to insti- tute reforms in the Adminietration. The Turks expected the Conference to yield, and now they are unusually serious, and consider the situation very grave." The gravity of the situation for Turkey is unquestionable. Reflecting persons naturally ask; was it to achieve this lame and impotent political conclusion, that the most powerful fleet in the world was sent out te Bunke Bay? Whom was it meant to intimidate? Whose good behaviour was it intended to enforoe. Not that of Russia surely ? For this we have Sir Stafford Northeote's assurance, eagerly urged on Wednesday at Liverpool. Sir Stafford " was contented to declare that the Ministry had never been animated by any unworthy jealousy of Rues, and he added that the suggestion of such a motive was a false and injurious accusation of their political enemies, which had done much mis- chief to their influence on the Continent." Sir S.Northcote is an honourable man, "so are they all all honourable men," but he imraly presumes a little on the weakneas of the national memory I What was the name of the Prime Minister who lately at the Guild- hall shook his fist in the face of Russia, and publicly bragged like a coarse political upstart, that England was not BS other nations, but could bear the out of as many campaigns as were necessary for her object. The spectacle in Besika Bay then was not meant no a means of persuasion to good be- haviour to Turkey, and Turkey therefore has not been persuaded. Turkey has probably thought she had good reason to believe that England was speaking with a double voice when it compared the Guildhall gasconade with the graver and more sober speech of the English Ambassador. The madmen of official Turkey have some reason to com- plain, for they seem to have been the victims of a huge delusion, bred and fostered in the slippery purlieu of Downing Street. One may well remember, however, that in the course of English history no Minister has been able for ever to evade the Nemesis of Parliament. Tergiversation and diplomatic treachery are not to be con- doned even by the epigrams of a Beacom- field.
